summary: US-C2b: The cache kill-switch - bypass availability caching at runtime, without a redeploy
description:
**Split out of TKT-205 at plan-final (2026-08-04).** It carries **epic TKT-31's third COS**: *"Kill-switch bypasses caches per service without redeploy."*

TKT-205 ships the in-memory availability cache. ADR-004's Consequences named the incident kill-switch as a requirement of that cache the moment it exists — *"needs staleness tests and a kill-switch to bypass caches during incidents"* — and TKT-205's plan showed the switch to be a second reviewable PR's worth of work on its own: a new credential threaded through `compose.yaml`, the `Makefile`, `scripts/smoke.sh` and two docs, plus a contract-declared control surface and its regeneration. A ticket cannot pass Gate 4 half-merged, so it is here rather than open across two PRs.

**Conditions of Success:**
- [ ] An operator can **disable** availability caching on a running inventory process, and **re-enable** it, **without a restart or redeploy**. Disabling purges what is cached and prevents in-flight loads started before the toggle from inserting.
- [ ] While disabled, every availability read reaches the store — proven by the same store-call counter TKT-205 uses, not by timing.
- [ ] The current state is **observable**: an operator can ask the running process whether the cache is on, and how much it holds.
- [ ] The control surface is **declared in `services/inventory/api/openapi.yaml`** (ADR-009), with generated code regenerated and **committed before** the gate.
- [ ] The credential decision is made explicitly and its **blast radius stated** (ADR-021: name the adversary). See the inherited context below.
- [ ] `make check` green.

**Inherited from TKT-205's plan draft — the design as `gpt-5.6-sol` proposed it, preserved so this ticket does not re-derive it:**
- `GET` / `PUT /internal/cache/availability`; PUT body `{"enabled": false}`; response reports `enabled`, `entries`, `in_flight`, `max_entries`, `max_entries_per_slot`, `ttl_seconds`. Responses `no-store`.
- A **new purpose-scoped credential** `INVENTORY_CACHE_CONTROL_TOKEN` / header `X-Inventory-Cache-Control-Token`, required at startup, **refused if equal to `INTERNAL_SERVICE_TOKEN`**, added only to inventory's Compose environment and never to the shared `&go-env` anchor. Rationale: the shared token opens commerce refunds and inventory operational holds, while this one controls only an availability/load trade-off.
- Disabling takes the cache lock, bumps every slot generation, purges, and makes subsequent reads call the source directly. Re-enabling starts cold.

**One open decision this ticket must settle, flagged at TKT-205's plan-review:**
The draft proposed answering **404** on a wrong or missing cache credential, matching the gateway's internal-route concealment and ADR-043's reasoning. But **inventory's existing `internalOnly` guard answers 401** (`services/inventory/internal/api/operational.go:22`), so adopting 404 for this one route would create a mixed convention *inside a single service* — which ADR-043 explicitly notes is already an unresolved inconsistency between catalog and commerce. Decide it deliberately: match inventory's existing 401, or change inventory's whole internal surface to 404. Do not split the difference silently.

**A second question worth answering before building:** is a *new* credential warranted at all? A holder of `INTERNAL_SERVICE_TOKEN` can already place operational holds and refund capacity on this service — strictly more powerful than disabling a cache. A narrower credential is worth its cost only if an operator exists who should be able to toggle the cache **without** those powers. Name that operator, or reuse `internalOnly` and say why.

Quality gates: `make check`; regenerated code committed before the gate.

objective.note: An operator can bypass availability caching on a running process during an incident, and see whether it is on.

scope.note: The control surface, its credential and its wiring. NOT the cache itself (TKT-205), NOT catalog's cache (TKT-206).

uncertainties.note: Two named decisions: 401-vs-404 on a wrong credential (inventory answers 401 today; the draft proposed 404), and whether a new purpose-scoped credential is warranted when INTERNAL_SERVICE_TOKEN already grants strictly more on this service. Both are stated in the description; under this run's waived gates the agent decides and records the rationale.

dependencies.note: Blocked by TKT-205 - there must be a cache to switch off.

approach.note: Inherited in full from TKT-205's plan draft; reproduced in the description so it is not re-derived.

first_slice.note: The availability cache is the only cache that exists after TKT-205; catalog's arrives in TKT-206 and reuses whatever this establishes.

success.note: Store-call counter while disabled, plus a state read. Both are assertions, not timings.

binding.rule: Local gate: `make check`. Commit regenerated code (`openapi_gen.go`, `api-types.gen.ts`) before running the gate - `check-generate` diffs against HEAD, so an uncommitted regen reads as drift and fails the run.
INTERNAL_SERVICE_TOKEN in the &go-env anchor: that one value opens every service's internal surface.

governingAdrs.why: Its Consequences name the incident kill-switch as a requirement the moment in-memory hot-event structures exist. This ticket is that clause.

Where a service auth guard lives: declared `security:` for the public contract, an inline check for the internal surface. Also the source of the 404-concealment argument - and of the note that catalog/commerce already disagree, which is why this ticket must not add a third convention.
Name the adversary before claiming a guarantee. A kill-switch credential's worth is exactly the difference between what it opens and what its holder could already do.
Contract-first: a new control endpoint must be declared in the OpenAPI document, and generated code regenerated and committed BEFORE the gate.
Response drift fails closed: any declared response header on the new operations is validated at runtime, so the handler and the declaration can only move together.

The full inherited design, and the reason for the split
The existing internal guard this must either match or deliberately depart from - it answers 401
The precedent for carving a narrower credential out of the shared token, and the comment explaining why

comments.body:
### Implementation readiness - CONCERNS

Split out of TKT-205 at plan-final (2026-08-04) rather than created from scratch, so its approach is inherited and its context-memo is baked. Moved straight to Ready under this run's waived Gate 1.

`risk:low` NOT claimed: a new operator surface, a credential decision with a stated blast radius, and an OpenAPI change with regeneration.

**Concern 1 (readiness `uncertainties`, owner human):** two auth-shaped decisions, both named in the description - 401 vs 404, and whether a new credential is warranted at all when `INTERNAL_SERVICE_TOKEN` already grants strictly more on this service. Under the waived gates the agent decides and records the rationale; flagged so the decisions stay visible rather than absorbed into an implementation.

**Concern 2:** this ticket is the epic's third COS in full. If it does not ship, TKT-31 cannot close - so it is not optional cleanup carved off to be forgotten.

**Claimed** by the agent, out of key order — and the reason is recorded on TKT-207's thread as a `kind=blocker` decision comment.

**Selection reason:** TKT-207's plan draft concluded that its COS 3 (the control case: cache off, counter tracks request count, flat assertion trips) **cannot be exercised faithfully without this ticket**. The alternative — a startup env toggle inside TKT-207 — was rejected because it would leave **two ways to disable one cache**, and the failure mode is the quiet one: an operator flips the runtime switch during an incident while a startup flag says otherwise. So TKT-207 returned to `Ready` with a `blocked-by` edge on this ticket, and this one moves up.

Nothing is lost by the reorder: **this ticket carries epic TKT-31's third COS**, so the epic cannot close without it either way.

**Blocker check:** TKT-210's `blocked-by` edge is TKT-205, **Done** and merged. Zero open blockers.

**Scope has grown since this ticket was split out of TKT-205, and that is restated here rather than left in the description:** at the split only inventory had a cache. **TKT-206 has since merged and catalog has one too.** This ticket must now cover **both services**, through one coherent mechanism — while ADR-045 deliberately declined to share code between the two caches, and records the extraction shape and trigger. Reconciling those is the plan's problem.

**Two hard requirements inherited from TKT-207**, which is now a consumer rather than a sibling:
- The surface must be **callable from a Go smoke test**, and must **report** state, not merely accept a toggle — TKT-207 reads the state back and requires both services to report disabled before running its control stage.
- It must manipulate **the same `enabled` state the cache read path actually consults.** A toggle that sets a flag the read path does not check would make TKT-207's control silently useless while looking green — the worst available outcome for a ticket whose entire purpose is evidence.

**Risk verdict: `risk:low` NOT claimed.**
- A new **operator surface** on two services, with a credential decision whose blast radius must be stated (ADR-021).
- An **OpenAPI change in two services**, so generated code must be regenerated and committed before the gate.
- Touching the read path of two caches that between them took **five adversarial review passes** and three [high] findings to get right. The `enabled` check has to sit where it cannot be bypassed, without disturbing the generation/single-flight logic underneath it.
- No money path, no data migration. The credential question is auth-adjacent: if the plan concludes a **new** credential is warranted, that is a change to the deployment's secret surface and is called out here in advance rather than discovered mid-implementation.

**Two decisions this ticket must settle rather than inherit**, both flagged in its readiness and both put to the drafter with their counter-arguments:
1. **Does a new purpose-scoped credential earn its keep?** TKT-205's draft proposed one. But a holder of `INTERNAL_SERVICE_TOKEN` can already place operational holds and refund capacity on inventory — being able to also disable a cache is **strictly less powerful than what they already hold**. A narrower credential is worth its cost only if an operator exists who should toggle the cache *without* those powers.
2. **401 or 404 on a wrong credential?** The draft proposed 404 for concealment (ADR-043). But inventory's existing `internalOnly` answers **401**, so adopting 404 for one new route would create a mixed convention inside a single service — and ADR-043 already records catalog/commerce disagreeing as something it chose not to churn.

---

**Gates waived for this run** — same standing owner instruction recorded on TKT-204 through TKT-207. `config.models` routing, cross-model review, TDD with tests observed red, `make check` green before every push and after the merge, and no AI attribution all stay in force.

Branch: `TKT-210-cache-kill-switch` off `origin/main`.

**Drafted by `gpt-5.6-sol`** (codex companion, `task --effort high`, read-only, **13m13s**) per `config.models.plan`.

> **Headline:** keep TKT-210 as **one cross-service ticket** — *"catalog and inventory need the same operational contract and TKT-207 must control them together."*

### Decision (a) — **reuse `INTERNAL_SERVICE_TOKEN`; no new credential**

> *"There is no identified cache-only operator at HEAD who should receive cache control without receiving the existing internal powers. A new credential therefore creates distribution, rotation, startup validation, Compose, and incident-response cost without reducing privilege for any real principal."*

It engages the back-office precedent and separates it: `CATALOG_STAFF_WRITE_TOKEN` exists because the back office is a **public-facing SSR process**, so its compromise must not open every service's internal surface. Nothing comparable receives cache control here.

**Blast radius, stated:** the capability writes no database rows; its holder can purge both caches and force public reads onto Postgres, bounded by each cache's existing semaphore and timeout — *"an availability/DB-load capability… can be abused as a denial-of-service amplifier."* The same credential already authorises **materially stronger** operations: inventory operational holds, capacity changes, refund returns, catalog seat-pin mutations. Authentication of a shared machine credential, **not** individual attribution.

### Decision (b) — **401 in both services**

Matches inventory's `internalOnly` and catalog's inline internal checks, and avoids a 401/404 split *within* a service. The gateway's edge concealment is unchanged: `/api/<svc>/internal/…` still returns 404. *"Changing both services' complete internal surfaces to 404 would be broad unrelated churn, and ADR-043 explicitly left catalog's 401 convention in place."*

### The mechanism — and the subtle part

Implementations stay separate per ADR-045 (the third-cache extraction trigger has not occurred). Each cache gains `enabled bool` (default true) and **`switchGen uint64` — a cache-control generation independent of the existing slot / list-detail generations**. Each flight captures it.

`SetEnabled` runs under the same mutex the reads use: flip `enabled`, bump `switchGen`, purge every entry (maintaining inventory's `perSlot` counts), leave running source calls alone. Idempotent on a no-op.

**Insertion requires all of:** enabled now · flight's `switchGen` current · the existing slot or list/detail generation still matching · source succeeded. The draft's reason for the extra generation is the case that would otherwise slip through:

> *"This matters when disable and re-enable occur before an old load finishes: checking only `enabled` would allow the old result to insert after re-enable."*

The read path checks `enabled` **on entry and again after acquiring the semaphore**. Disabled reads perform their own source call, return age zero, and never consult entries, join a flight, or insert.

### The operator surface

`GET`/`PUT /internal/cache-control` on **both** services, identical shape: `{"enabled":bool}` in, `{"enabled":bool,"entries":int}` out; `200/400/401/500`; every 200 declares `Cache-Control: no-store`; operation ids `getCacheControl`/`putCacheControl`. Catalog uses `security: []` to opt out of its document-level staff-write scheme, then does the ADR-043 inline check. Inventory mounts through its existing `internalOnly`. **Not routed through the gateway.**

> *"The handlers operate through the same `s.avail` or `s.public` object used by public reads. Extend those existing narrow interfaces… do not add a second flag or controller object that could drift from the read path."*

**A test caveat worth keeping:** *"Tests must use schema-valid bodies when asserting auth so a request-validation 400 cannot satisfy the test accidentally."*

### The TKT-207 seam — and an infrastructure gap it exposes

**Catalog has no host-published port**, and its internal route cannot pass through the gateway. So the ticket must add a loopback-only catalog port (`compose.yaml`, `scripts/smoke.sh`), following the pattern inventory/commerce/payments/access already use. *"This is part of the ticket, not incidental test setup."*

`smoke/cache_control_test.go` provides `disableBothCaches` / `restoreBothCaches` for TKT-207 to reuse: **register cleanup before changing either service**, disable both, GET both and require `enabled:false`, hand control back. Restoration is idempotent and uses non-fatal reporting so a failure restoring one service still attempts and verifies the other after a `t.Fatalf`.

### Risks and limits
A holder can force sustained database reads (semaphores bound concurrency, they are not rate limiters) · a process left disabled stays on the database until enabled or restarted, and **restart defaults to enabled — the disabled state is deliberately not durable** · state is **process-local**, each replica addressed separately · disabling does **not** purge the storefront `PageDataCache`, a browser cache or a future CDN · an in-flight caller may still receive the result it started before the toggle, but it cannot be inserted or joined · `entries` is cardinality, not bytes · no tamper-evidence, no operator identity.

### Ticket issues
1. *"'Per service' currently means per running process."* If it were meant to be one command controlling every replica, the ticket is underspecified and would need a control plane outside ADR-044/045's process-local design.
2. Catalog's missing host port is a real prerequisite, not test scaffolding.

**Critique by `main-agent` (Claude Opus 5)** per `config.models.planReview`.

### Verified

| Claim | Verdict |
|---|---|
| Both services answer **401** on their internal guards | **True.** Inventory `operational.go:19-24`; catalog's inline checks at `server.go:209/230/257`. Commerce is the 404 outlier, and ADR-043 explains why — a **compromised back office** holds a narrow commerce credential and could enumerate. **No such holder exists for inventory or catalog**, which is ADR-043's own stated reason for leaving catalog at 401. So 401 here is not merely consistent, it is the same reasoning reaching the same answer |
| Catalog has **no** host-published port | **True.** `compose.yaml` publishes loopback ports for inventory (`8091`), commerce (`8092`), payments (`8093`) and access (`8094`). Catalog is the only service without one — it is the odd one out, so adding it follows the established pattern rather than inventing deploy config |
| A new credential would not reduce privilege for any real principal | **Agreed, and I reached the same conclusion independently before reading the draft.** A holder of `INTERNAL_SERVICE_TOKEN` can already place operational holds and refund capacity on inventory. Disabling a cache is **strictly less powerful than what they already hold** |
| The `switchGen` argument | **Accepted, and it is the sharpest point in the draft.** Disable → re-enable while an old load is in flight would let a pre-disable result insert afterwards if only `enabled` were checked. The existing slot / list-detail generations do not move on a toggle, so they cannot catch it |

### Amendment 1 — cut the spec-parity test

The draft proposes `TestCacheControlContractsMatch` in the smoke package, comparing both specs' path items — while noting it *"needs no stack"*.

Two problems, and they compound: a test that needs no stack must not live in `smoke`, which is filtered out of `make test-go` and only runs behind Docker (the lesson TKT-204 already paid for). And relocating it needs a home, since it belongs to neither service.

**Cut it.** The live smoke test toggles both running services and requires both to report disabled — that proves the surfaces *work*, which is what TKT-207 depends on. Spec parity is a cosmetic property whose failure mode is already caught behaviourally. Recorded as a deliberate cut, not an oversight.

### Amendment 2 — the structural guards will fire, and that is the point

Both services carry a test asserting that only the public display handlers may reach the cache collaborator (`TestOnlyTheDisplayReadTouchesTheCache`, `TestOnlyTheMinuteTierPublicReadsUseTheCache`). Adding cache-control handlers that legitimately touch it **will** fail them until their allowlists name the new handlers.

That is the guard working, and the allowlist edit is the decision it forces. **The edit must add exactly the two control handlers and nothing broader** — no wildcard, no removing the check.

### Amendment 3 — `compose.yaml` and `scripts/smoke.sh` are deploy-adjacent; flagging deliberately

This run's standing instruction says to stop if implementation would touch CI/deploy config **in a way the ticket and plan did not anticipate**. This touches `compose.yaml` and `scripts/smoke.sh`, so I am recording why it is not a stop:

- It is **anticipated** — the plan names it, and the ticket's COS require an operator surface reachable by an operator and by TKT-207's control.
- It is **loopback-only** (`127.0.0.1:`), matching four existing services exactly. No new external exposure, no new credential, no CI workflow change.
- Without it, catalog's cache has no kill-switch at all, and **epic COS 3 says "per service"** — so omitting catalog fails the COS rather than trimming scope.

### Amendment 4 — say what "without redeploy" actually buys

The draft's limits list is good and one item deserves promotion into the operator documentation rather than only the ADR-adjacent prose: **the disabled state is not durable — a restart re-enables the cache.** An operator disabling a cache mid-incident and then rolling the service will silently get the cache back. That is defensible (fail-safe toward the designed behaviour) but it must be written where an operator reads it, not only where a reviewer does.

### Rejected — nothing

### Pre-mortem
1. **The toggle sets a flag the read path does not consult** — TKT-207's control then passes while proving nothing. *Guarded* by routing control through the same `s.avail`/`s.public` object, and by counting store calls while disabled rather than trusting the reported state.
2. **A smoke test leaves a cache disabled**, poisoning every later test in the run. *Guarded* by registering cleanup **before** the first mutation and by non-fatal, idempotent restoration of both services.
3. **An auth test passes on a request-validation 400** rather than the guard's 401. *Guarded* by the draft's own rule: schema-valid bodies when asserting auth.
4. **Disable→re-enable lets a stale load insert.** *Guarded* by `switchGen`.
5. **Someone reads "kill-switch" as protection against load.** It is not a rate limiter; the ADR limits and the operator doc must say so.

**The `kind=plan` draft as amended below is the plan.** Delta only.

### Amendments from plan-review
1. **Cut** the spec-parity smoke test — a stackless test must not live in the Docker-gated `smoke` module, and its property is already covered behaviourally.
2. The two structural cache-ownership guards **will** fail until their allowlists name the new control handlers; the edit adds exactly those two and nothing broader.
3. `compose.yaml` / `scripts/smoke.sh` are touched **deliberately and anticipated** — see decision 3.
4. "Restart re-enables the cache" goes into the **operator documentation**, not only the risk list.

### Decisions made by the agent under the waived Gate 2

**Decision 1 — reuse `INTERNAL_SERVICE_TOKEN`; no new credential.** The critique recommends it and I reached it independently. The deciding argument is not cost: **a new credential would not reduce anyone's privilege.** Its intended holder — the platform operator and the smoke harness — already holds a token that authorises operational holds, capacity changes and refund returns. A narrower credential is worth its distribution, rotation and startup-validation cost only if a principal exists who should toggle a cache *without* those powers, and none does at HEAD. The back-office precedent (`CATALOG_STAFF_WRITE_TOKEN`) is genuinely different: that process is public-facing SSR, so its compromise must not open every internal surface.

**Decision 2 — 401 in both services.** Matches what both already do. ADR-043's 404 concealment argument is specific to a principal who could enumerate — the compromised back office holding a narrow commerce credential — and that ADR explicitly left catalog at 401 for exactly the reason that applies here too: *"nothing hands out a narrow catalog credential… so there is no holder positioned to enumerate it."* Adopting 404 would create the intra-service split ADR-043 declined to churn.

**Decision 3 — catalog gets a loopback port; this ticket covers both services.** Epic COS 3 says the kill-switch works **per service**, and catalog now has a cache. Covering only inventory would fail the COS, not trim it. The change follows four existing services exactly and is loopback-only. **Flagged prominently because it is deploy-adjacent**: under this run's terms I am recording it as anticipated by the plan rather than treating it as a surprise, and it introduces no external exposure, no credential and no CI change.

**Decision 4 — keep it one ticket.** The critique recommends it: both services need the *same* operational contract, and TKT-207 must disable them together in one gate run. Splitting by service would leave TKT-207 blocked on the second half anyway.

### Introduced at plan-review, reviewed by no second model
1. **Cutting the spec-parity test** (amendment 1). Mine.
2. **The ADR-043 reading in decision 2** — that its 404 argument is about a *holder who can enumerate*, and that its own words about catalog apply here. The draft reached 401 by consistency; the reasoning is mine and it is what makes the decision principled rather than conventional.
3. **Amendment 3's deploy-config justification.** Mine, and it is the item an owner reviewing a gateless run would most want to see argued rather than assumed.
4. **Amendment 4** — moving the non-durable-disable warning into operator docs.

### `risk:low` — not claimed
Unchanged: a new operator surface on two services, OpenAPI changes with four regenerated files, a compose/smoke change, and edits to the read path of two caches that took five adversarial passes between them.

**Gate 2 waived by the repo owner; the agent proceeds to Building.**

**Implemented by `main-agent` (Claude Opus 5)** per `config.models.implement`. TDD.

```yaml
stage: coding
implementer: main-agent (Claude Opus 5)
branch: TKT-210-cache-kill-switch
commits: f7fca2c3, plus the coverage-gate fix
pr: https://github.com/mathd/ticketing_system/pull/171
gate: make check — EXIT=0, clean log (includes the Docker smoke suite)
spec_change: inventory only (its own convention); catalog hand-mounted undeclared (its own convention)
```

### TDD — red observed before every implementation

- Inventory cache tests first → `svc.SetEnabled undefined`, `st.Enabled undefined`. Then the switch.
- Catalog cache tests first → `c.SetEnabled undefined`, `c.Status undefined`. Then the switch.
- The HTTP tests were written against routes that did not exist and answered 404.

**And the tests caught a real bug in my own first implementation.** After wiring inventory's switch, `TestDisablePurgesAndBypassesTheCache` failed with *"source called 6 times after re-enable, want 5"*. Cause: the flight constructor did not capture `switchGen`, so `f.switchGen` stayed 0 while the cache's had advanced — **nothing ever inserted after any toggle**. Worth recording because the toggle-cycle test passed the whole time, vacuously: with nothing inserting, "a pre-toggle load must not insert" is trivially true. It was the *positive* test that caught it.

### One deviation from plan-final, decided during implementation

The plan said to declare the surface in **both** services' OpenAPI documents. On reaching catalog I found its Router's own comment: internal routes there are *"service-to-service, not part of the public OpenAPI contract; the response validator skips undeclared paths"* — `getTicketType`, `getPublishedPerformance`, `getPoolOfferState`, `pinSeats` are all hand-mounted and undeclared.

Declaring cache-control would have made it **the only declared internal route in catalog** — the same kind of intra-service inconsistency I refused for 401-vs-404 two paragraphs earlier in the same plan. So each service keeps its own convention: inventory declares (as it always does), catalog does not (as it never does). Behaviour is identical; only the convention differs. This also removed catalog's spec change and three regenerated files from the diff.

### Mutation checks — 7, each red then restored

| # | Mutation | Result |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Inventory read path ignores the switch | `TestADisabledReadDoesNotJoinAnInFlightLoad` FAILS: *"a disabled read returned 10 — it joined a load started before the cache was disabled"* |
| 2 | Inventory `switchGen` guard removed | `TestAToggleCycleRejectsALoadThatStartedBeforeIt` FAILS |
| 3 | Catalog read path ignores the switch | `TestADisabledPublicReadDoesNotJoinAnInFlightLoad` FAILS |
| 4 | Catalog `switchGen` guard removed | `TestAToggleCycleRejectsPreToggleLoads` FAILS |
| 5 | `SetEnabled` not idempotent (purges on a no-op) | `TestSetEnabledIsIdempotent` FAILS |
| 6–7 | (mutations 1 and 3, first attempt) | **Came back GREEN** — see below |

**Mutations 1 and 3 initially passed, and that mattered.** Neutering the read path's *first* `enabled` check changed nothing observable, which made it look like dead code — `SetEnabled` purges entries, so a disabled read always misses the entry map, and the post-semaphore re-check catches the rest.

It is not dead. **`SetEnabled` purges entries but does NOT clear the in-flight map**, and neither the slot nor the list/detail generation moves on a toggle. So without that first check a disabled reader finds a load started *before* the operator disabled the cache, joins it, and is served the exact value being withdrawn. Two tests were written for it — one per service — and mutations 1 and 3 then went red by name.

Third time in this epic that a mutation exposed a property with no test pinning it.

### Files

| File | Status |
|---|---|
| `services/inventory/internal/availability/cache.go` | `enabled`, `switchGen`, `SetEnabled`, `bypass`, `Status.Enabled` |
| `services/inventory/internal/api/cache_control.go` | new — handlers behind `internalOnly` |
| `services/inventory/api/openapi.yaml` + `openapi_gen.go` | route, schemas, `NeverCacheControl`; regenerated **and committed before** the gate |
| `services/catalog/internal/api/public_read_cache.go` | same switch, catalog-local per ADR-045 |
| `services/catalog/internal/api/cache_control.go` | new — hand-mounted, undeclared, inline auth |
| `smoke/cache_control_test.go` | new — live toggle of both services, plus the `disableBothCaches`/`restoreBothCaches` seam **TKT-207 consumes** |
| `compose.yaml`, `scripts/smoke.sh` | catalog's loopback port |
| `docs/development.md` | operator surface and its four limits |
| Both services' structural cache-ownership tests | allowlists name the two control handlers each — no wildcard |

### Two gate failures, different causes — neither a repeat

1. **`check-generate` drift** — regenerated `openapi_gen.go` was uncommitted, and the gate diffs against HEAD. The trap AGENTS.md documents in as many words; I hit it anyway.
2. **The smoke coverage gate (TKT-47)** — inventory's two declared operations were uncovered because my helper used a raw HTTP client and never reached `checkDirectServiceResponse`, the chokepoint that both contract-validates and records coverage.

The second fix made the surface *better* verified than my original: the contract declares `Cache-Control: no-store` required on both 200s, so ADR-028's validator now enforces it instead of one test asserting it.

**Reviewed by `gpt-5.6-sol`** (codex `adversarial-review`) per `config.models.aiReview`. **Two passes**, six findings, two [high]. Every finding verified against the revision under review before acceptance.

### Pass 1 — base `origin/main`: 4 findings (2 [high], 2 [medium]), all real, all fixed

| # | Finding | Verification | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **[high]** Inventory readers can join a **pre-disable flight after re-enable** | Both join predicates compared only `f.gen`; `SetEnabled` advances only `switchGen`. Confirmed by reading both call sites | **CONFIRMED → fixed** |
| 2 | **[high]** Same in catalog | Same shape, both branches | **CONFIRMED → fixed** |
| 3 | **[medium]** Catalog accepts **concatenated JSON** and changes state | Its route is hand-mounted, so outside request validation, and a plain `Decode` reads one value and ignores the rest. `httpx.DecodeJSON` (which inventory uses) *does* check for `io.EOF` — verified at `shared/go/httpx/json.go:24` | **CONFIRMED → fixed** |
| 4 | **[medium]** Smoke cleanup **aborts before restoring the second cache** | `cacheControlSet` calls `t.Fatalf` = `runtime.Goexit`, which `recover` cannot catch. My comment claimed it attempted both services; it did not | **CONFIRMED → fixed** |

**Findings 1 and 2 are the bug I fixed in TKT-205, reintroduced along a new axis.** There, a post-*invalidation* reader could join a pre-commit flight. Here it is a post-*re-enable* reader joining a pre-disable flight. Same mechanism, same blind spot: I guarded **insertion** and forgot that a joined flight **delivers its result directly**, never touching the cache.

And my own tests missed it for the same reason both times: `TestAToggleCycleRejects…` waits for the old load to **finish** before reading, so it only ever exercised insertion. The reviewer said so explicitly — *"The toggle-cycle test misses this because it waits for the old flight to finish before issuing the post-toggle read."*

Finding 4 is the sharper one about process: **my comment asserted a property the code did not have.** It said restoration attempted both services even if the first failed. It could not — and the consequence would have landed on whatever ran next in the suite, not on the failing test.

### Pass 2 — base `5d8d068f` (fix diff 1): 2 findings [medium], **both about the branch I added in round 1**

1. The new post-semaphore bypass **leaks its semaphore slot if the source panics** — no deferred release, and `net/http` recovers handler panics, so the process survives with permanently reduced capacity.
2. **No test pins that branch.** With the default 1000-slot semaphore nothing ever queues, so reverting it left every test green.

Both correct. And the second one is what made the right fix visible: I could not write a test that distinguished the branch's presence because **the branch was not doing anything**. A read that queues for a slot and finds the cache disabled cannot populate it either way — the insertion guard already requires `enabled`. All it added was avoiding a transient flight registration, plus a second place to leak a slot.

**So it was deleted rather than fixed**, in both services. Both findings went with it, and "disabled" is now decided in two places instead of three. The tests were replaced with the properties that actually hold, each mutation-checked on a **reachable** path:
- a read that acquires its slot after a disable cannot populate the cache (breaking the insert guard's `enabled` term fails it);
- the bypass path releases its slot even when the source panics (making the release inline fails it, by timeout).

The panic case earns its keep independently: a repeatable source panic would otherwise exhaust every slot until misses block forever — a cache disabled during an incident quietly becoming an outage.
